Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: This scoping review surveys quantitative online dating research from a media-market perspective.
We conceptualize online dating as online relationship search, which refers to twosided matching activities that capitalize features of online dating platforms as both media and markets.

Accordingly, we reviewed findings about the links between search strategies and outcomes, particularly covering a stream of strategies aimed to unleash the potential of online dating as media-markets: endorsing online dating as a venue for relationship search, expanding access to market options, optimizing matching procedures, and enhancing mutual understanding via interaction.
A total of 134 studies were included via manual and computerized screening.

First, pre-2010s research tended to find meeting a partner via an online dating site associated with higher relationship quality whereas post-2010s research often showed dating apps associated with less favorable search outcomes.
Second, both excessive and inadequate access to options were found to be counterproductive.
Third, meta-cognition about matching procedures were found to enhance matching outcomes.
Fourth, daters were found to leverage different communication modalities/affordances for achieving different goals (garnering attention vs. facilitating long-term development).
Findings suggest that successful searches can be facilitated by strategies that capitalize media market potential at different stages of search.
We discuss how the media-market perspective may contribute to future work.

Online dating has intrigued communication scholars: it goes beyond being merely a topic of research but provokes impactful thoughts and theories about how mediation communication shapes relationship development.

Specifically, scholars have theorized relationship development in online dating by studying the effect of endorsing online dating as a meeting venue (e.g., Hu et al., 2024; Sharabi & Dorrance-Hall, 2024), increased choice size (e.g., D'Angelo & Toma, 2017; M. F. text.text: We will fill this gap: whereas the EAMC framework helps to categorize different findings, the media-market perspective offers a lens to coherently interpret and integrate EAMC-relevant findings to design better platforms that help daters strategize and strengthen their search.

In this scoping review, we as social scientists will survey existing studies that directly, quantitatively examined the links between relationship search strategies that are relevant to endorsing online dating as a meeting venue, expanding market access, optimizing matching, and enhancing interaction and relationship outcomes of such search.
In reviewing them, we aim to describe the area, understand what was found for each media-market-relevant strategies, and inform theoretical advancements.
We used both manual and computerized screening to achieve objective judgments.
Specific analysis of included papers remained fully manual.
Below, we first introduce the media-market perspective, briefly define components of online relationship search, and state the task of this work.
We define online dating (platforms) as media-markets.

By media-market, we mean a form of social structure where two-sided matching market activities are mediated by communication technology (Hu & Markowitz, 2026; Oyer, 2014; Roth, 2015); relational communication operates within such structure-that is, communication is shaped by the affordances and constraints of such structure (Bourdieu & Wacquant, 1992; Monge, 1973).

text.text: While markets are abstract, rule-based structure that governs relationship search, media are tangible infrastructure that is closer to subjective experience, which is the direct object of daters' attempts to strategize their search (i.e., to gain better media use experiences).
Thus, we will not only organize this review under EMAC, but also pay close attention to strategies that people leverage to transform their media use experiences.
Together, it stands to reason that the media-market conceptualization informs a more structural understanding of online relationship search.

The conceptualization helps to reveal overarching structural forces while preserving possibilities of change via media use strategies; it anchors around such phenomenologically sensible strategies while situate such strategies within structural affordances and constrains.
Indeed, it would be what Bourdieu and Wacquant (1992) called, a structural constructivist view.

Next, we begin to define online relationship search strategies under EAMC to understand specific areas that this review covers.
The first component in online relationship search is naturally entering media-markets: endorsing online dating as a way of meeting others.
Does endorsing online dating as a meeting venue improve or worsen relationship search outcomes?
This question pertains to the general function of online dating as media-markets.

Two competing predictions can be found for the link between online dating endorsement (e.g., meeting a partner in online dating vs. offline, or using online dating more vs. less) and relationship search outcomes.
One prediction carries a positive tone and suggests that online dating is associated with more satisfying relationships (e.g., Cacioppo et al., 2013).

Each prediction comes with good reasoning.
Thus, it will be valuable to review what the empirical evidence from different research traditions or approaches has said about the effect of online dating endorsement.
We ask: RQ1: How is online dating endorsement related to relationship search outcomes?
In addition to probing the effect of entering the media-market of online dating, it helps to examine effects of specific, downstream strategies.
The next group of strategies are about expanding access to dating options, commonly studied in research of partner choice (e.g., "Does having more mate options benefit search outcomes?").

Though choice is used to name a research area, it helps to distinguish choice as an outcome (i.e., the person that one chooses to date from a pool of persons) from options (i.e., a pool of persons that are available for selection).

Market economists favor thick markets (markets with abundant options) over thin markets (markets that are under-optioned) because thick markets host more diverse option and searchers with different preferences and traits are more likely to find a compatible option (Roth, 2015).

text.text: Additionally, the mate evaluation theory (MET; Eastwick et al., 2023) questions whether matching (vs. not matching) in traits and preferences dictates relationship quality.

text.text: Therefore, the relationship between uses of matching strategies and relationship search outcomes is likely complicated.
There are merits in knowing how empirical work has found out about this association.
We propose: RQ3: How are matching strategies related to relationship search outcomes?
The last component in online relationship search is to foster mutual understanding via strategic communication in media-markets.
Communication here means verbal or nonverbal interaction between two online daters, ranging from viewing content in someone's profile to talking in an offline date (Sharabi, 2024).
text.formatted: Communication here means verbal or nonverbal interaction between two online daters, ranging from viewing content in someone's profile to talking in an offline date <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Sharabi, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Communication is central to uncertainty reduction and building a compatible relationship (Berger, 1979; Eastwick & Joel, 2025).
text.formatted: Communication is central to uncertainty reduction and building a compatible relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Berger, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Eastwick & Joel, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Though computermediated communication allows people to selectively present themselves, by writing a witty biography in one's profile, choosing a filtered photo, or sending humorous text messages, using any strategy alone may not guarantee a successful relationship search; for example, attraction often drops when daters switch from online to face-to-face (FtF) communication (e.g., Hancock & Toma, 2009; Ramirez et al., 2015; Sumner et al., 2025).

text.text: Given the volume and centrality of research examining communication strategies in online dating, it is beneficial to understand roles of these strategies in online relationship search.
We propose: RQ4: How are communication strategies related to relationship search outcomes?
Taken together, the media-market perspective of online dating leads to four questions that help to draw insights from existing perspectives and findings about online relationship search.
Each question pertains to one step in the chain process.
We present this process and key concerns conceptually in Figure 1.
text.formatted: We present this process and key concerns conceptually in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>.

text.text: The media-market perspective, again, is aimed to offer an underexplored, structural constructivist view that can derive practical strategies within mediamarket constraints and guide future work.

Anchoring around the specific link between media-market search strategies and search outcomes, this scoping review surveys studies that generate direct findings regarding such links (thus not being aimed to include every impactful study in online dating).
These findings will be reviewed to generate directions for future work.
Non-strategic predictors that represent stable traits fall beyond our focus.

Given traits like how people look, their socio-economic status, race, biological sex, attachment styles cannot be easily altered in a short time, or at all; findings about these traits are not about strategies per se.

By contrast, strategies are approaches to online dating that people can adjust in a short time (e.g., spending more time in online dating, migrating to a platform with more mate options or a different matching procedure, communicating in a certain way).

Therefore, though trait-like findings are valuable, the media-market perspective led us to only focus on studies that have examined predictors translatable to strategies (though strategies may not be the only concern in these studies).
To understand the reviewed studies, we will also describe their topic distribution and methodology.

Thus, we propose the fifth research question, which will be answered first given the way we present our results: RQ5: How are the associations between media-market strategies and online relationship search outcomes studied?

text.text: We also manually checked for missing papers by screening ten most cited papers in each database's search results to see whether eligible papers in their reference and citation list were included.
This procedure added another six papers.
Removing duplicate articles, we found 1413 papers remained for title and abstract screening.

text.text: Inclusion criteria applied in this process are: the article needed to (a) be an peer-reviewed journal article, (b) examine online dating strategies (i.e., approaches to online dating that can be adjusted within a short time), (c) report relational outcome (i.e., cognition, emotion, and behavior indicative of the progression of a relationship initiated through online dating), (d) examine the link between online dating strategies and relational outcomes, (e) have been published between January 1, 1996 and April 1, 2026, (f) be written in English, (g) report an original empirical quantitative research that aims to generate general abstract knowledge (vs. usability test of apps) 4 .
Accordingly, exclusion criteria specify articles that fall beyond our scope, which are correspondent opposites of inclusion criteria.
For example, exclusion criteria for b is an article that did not examine online dating use at all; all its predictors were non-strategy (e.g., attachment style, physical attractiveness).
One author manually screened all searched, non-redundant papers.

The screening results were verified by Claude AI to ensure objective judgment that follows the inclusion and exclusion criteria (model: Sonnet 4.6; mode: extensive thinking, which is suitable for complex tasks).
Reliability was assessed and both (human) authors discussed and resolved conflicts.

text.text: Specifically, we wrote a prompt (Appendix A) for Claude AI to select eligible papers based on title and abstract screening.
Temperature was set at 0 (strictly following our prompt; low randomness) and top p was set at 1 (fully exploring topic distribution).
Trials of dozens of articles were conducted iteratively until coding outcomes met criteria.
Claude AI and the first author then independently screened all 1413 papers by title and abstract.
Intercoder agreement reached 96% (substantial agreement) and reliability reached Krippendorf α=0.84 (reliable coding).
The second author randomly sampled 10% of all papers to verify the results by independently screening sampled papers and compared results between three coders.
Agreement rate was 95% and Krippendorf's α=.85.
Both authors then addressed conflicts in screening results strictly based on the criteria.

Over 90% of conflicts resulted from AI being overly lenient and included papers that examined baseline demographics-related mating preferences using online dating data without an online dating-related predictor.
They fell beyond the scope of this review and were excluded. 176 papers were included for full-text screening.
The full content of these papers was retrieved for full-text screening, which followed the same procedures.
The prompt (Appendix A) was refined through trials and fed to Claude to screen all 176 papers for eligibility; meanwhile, the first author screened the same papers independently.
The first author verified their screening results with AI's results.
Agreement reached 91%.
Krippendorf's α was .80 (reliable coding).
The second author randomly sampled 10% of all papers to screen independently and compared results between three coders.
Agreement rate was 88% and Krippendorf's α=.82.
Conflicts were resolved by both authors per criteria.

Papers were excluded for not examining online dating use (n=46), not including a relational outcome (n=15), not examining the relationship between online dating use and relational outcomes (n=1), not being a quantitative study (n=2), and being outdated (e.g., retracted; n=2).
A total of 110 papers were included.
The authors manually added two papers through reference and citation checks that were run through the 110 papers.
A total of 112 papers were included for analysis.
Some papers reported more than one study, so a sum of 134 studies were analyzed further.
We acknowledge that our criteria led to a very specific focus pertaining to our theoretical concerns.
Some valuable, foundational, and impactful online dating research may therefore not have been included because they fall beyond our scope.
Proceeding to analysis, we coded descriptive variables of half of all included studies.

Key variable included Strategy of Focus (endorsing online dating as a meeting venue, expanding access to mate options, optimizing matching, enhancing communication), Relationship Outcome, Design (randomized controlled trials or RCT, randomized field experiment, non-RCT experiment, survey, non-obtrusive study, simulation), Duration, Channel (dating app, dating website, both, or unspecified), Sample Unit, Sample Size, and Sample Demographics (age, gender, sexual orientation, relationship status, geographic area).
To answer RQ1-4, we coded the actual predictor(s) and relationship outcome(s) in each study, with test statistics where available.

text.text: With these sampling characteristics in mind, we move onto presenting main findings from these studies.
Examining the links between strategies and outcomes, RQ1 was concerned with the relationship between online dating endorsement and relationship outcomes.

First, meeting a partner in online dating (vs. offline dating) was associated with less satisfying, stable, or successful relationships (Bleize et al., 2023; Blunt-Vinti et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2024; Kowal et al., 2025; Langlais & Lee, 2025; Sharabi & Dorrance-Hall, 2024).

text.text: A candidate presented on a dating app was also seen less trustworthy than a candidate presented on a non-dating social app (e.g., social networking sites; Silva et al., 2019).

text.text: Meeting a partner in online dating was also associated with more perceived societal marginalization and lower social network support (Sharabi & Dorrance-Hall, 2024).

text.text: Higher compulsive dating app use was likewise associated with more subjective online success (Gao et al., 2024) but lower firstdate satisfaction (Vera Cruz et al., 2023) or commitment (Hu, 2024a).

text.text: Second, online dating was associated with more opportunities to form a relationship with people who are similar or different.
Two people in a relationship that began in online dating were more likely to have a similar education background (Potarca, 2017 (Potarca, , 2021;; Qian & Hu, 2025).

text.text: Mixed findings were found for the associations between online dating and homogamy in other demographics (e.g., age, religion, race; Kornrich & Robbins, 2024; Potarca, 2017; Qian & Hu, 2025; R. J. Thomas, 2020).

text.text: Two mechanisms were raised in these studies: selection, by which online dating allows people to select a mate of a certain demographic, and constraint, by which online dating frees people from being stuck with mates of a certain demographic only.
However, it is worth pointing out that most studies examining the relational correlates of online dating endorsement were cross-sectional.
This limitation prevents drawing causal conclusions and may have introduced selection bias and confounds.

It is possible that people who chose to find a relationship via online dating faced greater romantic constraints prior to online dating than people who chose to meet someone via offline dating; these traits are rarely controlled in a cross-sectional study commonly relying on large-scale survey data.
Longitudinal studies, particularly ones that employed stricter causal inference approaches (propensity score matching, difference-in-difference) were rarer.

Together, a negative association between endorsing online dating and quality of searched relationship seems to have emerged, but it is too soon to conclude that online dating makes poorer relationships.
Having reviewed findings of online dating endorsement, we turn to reporting findings about specific online dating strategies.
RQ2 was concerned with access to dating options.
There was no universal choice effect.
Some evidence suggests that having more dating options was associated with or led to lower match participation (Fong, 2024) and lower relational pursuit (D'Angelo & Toma, 2017, delayed effect).
text.formatted: Some evidence suggests that having more dating options was associated with or led to lower match participation (Fong, 2024) and lower relational pursuit (D'Angelo & Toma, 2017, delayed effect).

text.text: Some evidence suggests that online daters preferred to have more options (Lenton et al., 2008, Study 1), and that having more options led to more option-searching activities (Wu & Chiou, 2009), higher match compatibility and similarity (Hu & Markowitz, 2026), higher relational pursuit (Hu & Markowitz, 2026), and higher commitment readiness (Hu, 2024a; Hu & Markowitz, 2026).

text.text: Studies also reported a non-significant association between the number of dating options and relationship outcomes (D'Angelo & Toma, 2017: immediate effect; Lenton et al., 2008, Study 2; Lenton & Stewart, 2008; Pronk & Denissen, 2020; Sculley et al., 2021).

text.text: Contrary to a common expectation, having more options was not consistently associated with being more selective (Hu & Markowitz, 2026; Shi et al., 2025; Wu & Chiou, 2009).

text.text: Evidence also suggests that people like having all options presented simultaneously (which is a more dated design in online dating) rather than sequentially (which is a more contemporary design), which was indicated by feeling more satisfied and less regretful with the person they chose (Bischof et al., 2025).

text.text: Indeed, one paper reported that people increased their rejection as they went through a sequence of choice (Pronk & Denissen, 2020).

text.text: The studies examining choice effects were often experimental, thus offering causal evidence.

However, context differed between studies: options were operationalized as an imagined number of options, vignette-style profiles, or profiles on real-time online dating platforms; evaluations were made immediately after choice was made, some time after the choice was made, or even without making a choice; the variety of options also differed, with available social information being lean in some studies and rich in others.
Such variation may explain why effects differed across studies.
With expanded choice sets, examining efficient matching procedures can be important (RQ3).

Though matching involves complicated computational procedures, studies showed that being mindful of the matching process and a dating candidate's availability are often associated with better matching outcomes.

First, higher trust in dating algorithms was associated with more favorable relationship appraisal and higher relational pursuit online (Cho & Sundar, 2022; Hu & Oh, 2025; Sharabi, 2021a; Tong et al., 2016) and after the first date (Sharabi, 2021a); higher trust in algorithms was also associated with a higher likelihood of being in a relationship found in online dating among past online daters (Hu, 2024b).

text.text: Higher awareness or knowledge of algorithms was associated with lower difficulty in searching for a mate in online dating (Hu & Zhan, 2024).
text.formatted: Higher awareness or knowledge of algorithms was associated with lower difficulty in searching for a mate in online dating <ref type="bibr">(Hu & Zhan, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the use of different matching procedures can make a difference too.

Online daters experienced higher matching success when availability of a potential partner (in terms of the ability or probability of accepting one's matching request or replying to their message) was considered in the design.
Specifically, this was achieved through highlighting partner availability to users (N. Huang et al., 2022; J. Jung et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Specifically, this was achieved through highlighting partner availability to users <ref type="bibr">(N. Huang et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">J. Jung et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, highlighting users' availability or commitment to a potential partner (e.g., by allowing users to propose a match with a rose, which is a scarce resource) can also enhance matching success (Bapna et al., 2016 (Bapna et al., , 2023;; Lee et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Interestingly, highlighting users' availability or commitment to a potential partner (e.g., by allowing users to propose a match with a rose, which is a scarce resource) can also enhance matching success <ref type="bibr">(Bapna et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Bapna et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lee et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, availability information could be used through having algorithms considered daters' availability when recommending matches (Bojd & Yoganarasimhan, 2022; Celdir et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Kleinerman et al., 2021; Krzywicki et al., 2015).

text.text: These studies suggest that availability information functions as an important signal that improves matching success.

However, there is a disconnection between small-scale studies that examined placebo effects of matching-related cognition (e.g., trust in algorithms) and large-scale studies that tested mechanical effects of particular matching procedures on real or simulated online dating platforms.
It is highly plausible that both play a role in online relationship search, yet few studies examined both.

Social theories that explain what happens between input and output in matching seem particularly lacking in the latter studies, though the end goal of studies examining matching is to decode what is hidden in the black box of matching in online dating.
Not less important than gaining access to dating options or being matched with compatible options, online daters need to communicate with a chosen match to build relationships (RQ4).

Communication is defined as verbal and nonverbal interaction, including crafting one's profile and browsing others' profiles, exchanging messages online, and communicating via other modalities (e.g., video chat or FtF; Frost et al., 2008; Sharabi & Caughlin, 2017; Sharabi & Dykstra-DeVette, 2019).

text.text: Overall, the rich literature focusing on communication strategies generated diverse insights.
From a media-market perspective, these insights can be understood as about how social information can be strategically distorted and restored to fit certain needs in relationship development.

For example, many findings reveal the effect of strategically presenting one's desirable traits on garnering further interaction; other findings explain how the revelation of previously under-represented social information impact mate evaluation over the course of relationship initiation.
Ultimately, communication strategies are often aimed at (creating opportunities for) fostering understanding between market players, with a common goal of producing a stable match.
As we mentioned, communication (e.g., self-disclosure) helps people construct mutual understanding, thus creating perception of a stable match.
Notwithstanding this possibility, the media-market perspective will revise what is considered "successful communication".

Contrary to the common assumption that a positive outcome means two people like each other after interaction, the media-market perspective will suggest that disillusion (e.g., losing interest as one learns more about another) can be a favorable outcome for finding a stable match too.
Market transactions are all-about timely gauging of mutual interest and moving on from mismatches quickly, where communication strategies play important roles.
From a novel, media-market perspective, this scoping review addresses the connection between media-market strategies and online relationship search outcomes.

Findings suggest merits in understanding online dating from a media-market perspective, where daters strategize media use strategies to capitalize potentials of media-markets (i.e., online dating platforms) and optimize outcomes of relationship search.

Below, we briefly discuss how the media-market perspective helps to make sense of the reviewed findings and propose four emerging questions in online dating research, each correspondent to one type of strategy.
We will then review how the media-market perspective contributes to advancing online dating research and broader field of mediated interpersonal communication.
We found that more studies point to a negative connection between endorsing online dating as a way of mate selection and relationship quality, particularly in recent years.
This contrasts earlier findings about online dating websites.

From a media-market perspective, this suggests that media-markets fail to function as expected, or that features of media-markets failed to be capitalized in daters' favor, such that market entry was associated with low or negative utility.

In market design theories, market failure is attributed to poor market designs-or in our case, poor media-market designs, which block access to options (e.g., hiding matches behind the paywall), distort signals (e.g., encouraging people to lie about their traits and preferences), and congest market (e.g., prioritizing popular daters over maximizing overall matching rates), among other malfunctions (Roth, 2015).

text.text: What would a media-market perspective recommend for research about online dating endorsement?
Technologies emerge every few years: social networking sites, online dating, chatbots, and so on.
A common scenario is that despite doubts these technologies get integrated into everyday lives eventually.

A media-market perspective would encourage research that promotes informed acceptance of these technologies, including online dating platforms, along with their latest features like AI-matchmaking, with questions like "Do users enter a new mediamarket by endorsing this new technology or feature?"
and "Are new media-markets functioning well-that is, is entry of such media-markets associated with higher utility for relationship search?"
To analyze how media-markets may be best designed for strategies to be useful, we turn to discussing specific strategies post media-market entry.
Our review gathers mixed findings about whether having more dating options propels or postpones relationship progression.

One salient feature of online dating as media-markets is that it can gives many more mate options that other venues for couples to meet; however, the number of mate options vary by platform design (Oyer, 2014).
text.formatted: One salient feature of online dating as media-markets is that it can gives many more mate options that other venues for couples to meet; however, the number of mate options vary by platform design <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Oyer, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The reviewed studies suggest that effects of having more options (i.e., choice effects) may not be universal but contingent upon conceptualization of option and research design.
This tension further shows the value of a media-market perspective (vs. a pure media or a pure market perspective).

A pure media perspective often suggests that human brains have not evolved to process excessive information that technology affords, thus predicting a negative choice effect on relationship development (e.g., D'Angelo & Toma, 2017; M. F. Thomas et al., 2026).

F. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Thomas et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This perspective is more focused on phenomenological experiences.

A pure market perspective would predict that more options mathematically host more diversity and afford higher match compatibility, thus predicting a positive choice effect (e.g., Oyer, 2014; Roth, 2015).

text.text: This view is more structural, which "puts agents on vacation" (Bourdieu & Wacquant, 1992).
text.formatted: This view is more structural, which "puts agents on vacation" <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bourdieu & Wacquant, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: The mixed findings in our work shows that a reconciliation between both views can be beneficial, and we suggest that the media-market perspective can help achieve that.
This review also shows that certain matching strategies make daters more engaged in the relationship initiation process.

Trust in algorithms seems to be beneficial for promoting a more pro-relationship approach in online dating (e.g., thinking and behaving in ways that do not help develop a relationship), which is suggested as a placebo effect in the literature (e.g., Hu & Oh, 2025).
text.formatted: Trust in algorithms seems to be beneficial for promoting a more pro-relationship approach in online dating (e.g., thinking and behaving in ways that do not help develop a relationship), which is suggested as a placebo effect in the literature (e.g., Hu & Oh, 2025).

text.text: Additionally, considering daters' availability seems to contribute to a higher matching efficiency: algorithm or interface design that considers such information (rather than merely how popular a user is) in recommendation processes can lead to more matching success.
We think this is a mechanical effect where algorithmic procedures are altered by different data input (vs. placebo effects).
Once again, there seems to be effects that are within control of individuals (trust in algorithms) and effects that are structural and agonistic to individuals' will (how algorithms match people).
Therefore, a media-market perspective can help strike a balance between accounting for individuals' experiences while situating those experiences in bigger market designs and structures.

It follows for future research to examine how individuals' cognition and behavior (e.g., trust in algorithm, mate evaluation) and market structure (circulation of available mates, matching mechanisms) interact to produce compatible matches.

Furthermore, communication is central to developing a satisfying relationship (Finkel et al., 2012), and this review suggests that choosing the right communication strategies for the right purpose is helpful.
text.formatted: Furthermore, communication is central to developing a satisfying relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Finkel et al., 2012)</ref>, and this review suggests that choosing the right communication strategies for the right purpose is helpful.

text.text: Strategic presentation seems rewarding to attracting attention while truthful disclosure seems beneficial for long-term development.
To sum up, the media-market perspective helps leverage the strengths of diverse existing perspectives by situating strategies to find a compatible match online within media-market designs.
Therefore, the media-market perspective to online dating is what Bourdieu and Wacquant (1992) suggest a "structural constructivist" view.
text.formatted: Therefore, the media-market perspective to online dating is what <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bourdieu and Wacquant (1992)</ref> suggest a "structural constructivist" view.

text.text: We have accordingly proposed four questions that help produce future research that examine online relationship research considering platforms as both media and markets, the process as capitalizing their designs using certain strategies, the success of such attempts as constrained by both individuals' capacity and structural conductivity.
We refrain from offering pragmatic implications.
This scoping review makes it clear that findings are very contingent upon boundary conditions that are not yet clarified.
More importantly, we follow Wacquant's (2026) principles for social theorists to separate scientific discovery from moralist judgment (i.e., assigning responsibilities to persons and institutions).
text.formatted: More importantly, we follow <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Wacquant's (2026)</ref> principles for social theorists to separate scientific discovery from moralist judgment (i.e., assigning responsibilities to persons and institutions).

text.text: We will leave the latter task to roles that are more fitting than social scientists.
Instead, we conclude this paper with limitations and future research directions.
While it is common for reviews to suggest that causal evidence is lacking in a field, this scoping review shows that online dating is advantageously full of experimental research.
The main limitation lies in an over-reliance on White, educated, industrial, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) samples, which are not uncommon in social sciences.
A more theoretical limitation, or rather, a future direction, is as we argue to integrate more individualist views with more structural views.
The forwarded media-market perspective has suggested a few potential directions for research production.
Hopefully, these directions will help capitalize the rich causal evidence in separate views through the integration of these views.

It stands to reason that communication in online relationship search can be viewed as media-market behaviors.
Whether a communication strategy (e.g., strategic self-presentation vs. truthful disclosure) is beneficial depends on whether it serves the media-market goal at hand.

That is, whether a communication strategy helps garner exposure to other market participants when attention is needed and whether a strategy helps build understanding or identifying unsuitable matches when compatibility-building is prioritized are important questions to consider.
Per the media-market perspective, future research may examine whether the strategy-goal match has an effect on online relationship search outcomes.
